paragraphs: “You are taking too many sins on yourself,” Mother would say, weeping.

“Mother, darling, I am crying for joy, not for grief. I cannot explain it to you, but I like to humble myself before them, because I do not know how to love them enough. If I have sinned against everyone, yet everyone forgives me too, and that is heaven. Am I not in heaven now?”

And he said a great deal more that I do not remember. I do remember going into his room once when nobody else was there. It was a bright evening, the sun was going down, and the whole room was full of light. He beckoned to me and I went over to him. He put his hands on my shoulders and looked into my face, tenderly and lovingly. He said nothing for a minute. He only looked at me like that.
“Well,” he said, “go and play now. Enjoy life for me too.”

So I went out and ran off to play. And many times in my life afterwards I remembered, even with tears, how he told me to enjoy life for him too. He had many other wonderful and beautiful sayings, though we did not understand them at the time. He died in the third week after Easter. He was fully conscious, though he could no longer speak, and he did not change up to his last hour. He looked happy. His eyes shone and searched for us, and he smiled at us and beckoned us. People talked a great deal about his death, even in the town. All this made an impression on me at the time, but not too deep a one, though I cried a good deal at his funeral. I was young then, only a child. Yet a lasting impression, a hidden feeling about it all, stayed in my heart, ready to rise up and answer when its time came. And so indeed it happened.
_(b) Of the Holy Scriptures in the Life of Father Zossima_

I was left alone with my mother. Her friends began to advise her to send me to Petersburg, as other parents did. “You have only one son now,” they said, “and a fair income. If you keep him here, you may be robbing him of a brilliant career.” They suggested that I be sent to Petersburg, to the Cadet Corps, so that I could afterwards enter the Imperial Guard. My mother hesitated for a long time, because it was dreadful to part with her only child. But at last she made up her mind, though not without many tears, believing that she was acting for my happiness. She brought me to Petersburg and placed me in the Cadet Corps, and I never saw her again. For she too died, three years later. She spent those three years mourning and grieving for both of us.

From the house of my childhood I have brought away nothing but precious memories, for no memories are more precious than those of early childhood in one’s first home. That is almost always so, as long as there is any love and harmony in the family at all. Indeed, precious memories can remain even from a bad home, if only the heart knows how to find what is precious. Among my memories of home I count my memories of the Bible, which I was very eager to read at home, child as I was. I had a book of Scripture history then, with excellent pictures, called _A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament_, and I learned to read from it. I have it on my shelf now, and I keep it as a precious relic of the past. But even before I learned to read, I remember being moved to devotion for the first time, at eight years old. My mother took me alone to the service on the Monday before Easter. (I do not remember where my brother was at the time.) It was a fine day, and I remember today, as though I saw it now, how the incense rose from the censer and floated softly upwards, and how, up in the cupola, it mingled in rising waves with the sunlight that streamed in at the little window. I was stirred by the sight, and for the first time in my life I consciously received the seed of God’s word in my heart. A youth came out into the middle of the church carrying a big book, so large that at the time I thought he could scarcely carry it. He laid it on the reading desk, opened it and began to read, and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something that was read in the church of God. In the land of Uz there lived a man, righteous and God-fearing, who had great wealth, so many camels, so many sheep and asses. His children feasted, and he loved them very much and prayed for them. “It may be that my sons have sinned in their feasting.” Now the devil came before the Lord together with the sons of God, and said to the Lord that he had gone up and down the earth and under the earth. “And have you considered my servant Job?” God asked him. And God boasted to the devil, pointing to His great and holy servant. And the devil laughed at God’s words. “Give him over to me and You will see that Your servant will murmur against You and curse Your name.” And God gave up the just man He loved so much to the devil. And the devil struck down his children and his cattle and scattered his wealth, all of a sudden, like a thunderbolt from heaven. And Job tore his mantle and fell down upon the ground and cried aloud, “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return into the earth. The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever and ever.”

Fathers and teachers, forgive my tears now, for all my childhood rises up again before me. I breathe now as I breathed then, with the breast of a little child of eight, and I feel as I did then: awe and wonder and gladness. The camels caught my imagination at that time. So did Satan, who talked like that with God, and God, who gave His servant up to destruction, and His servant crying out: “Blessed be Your name although You punish me.” Then came the soft, sweet singing in the church: “Let my prayer rise up before You,” and again the incense from the priest’s censer, and the kneeling and the prayer. Ever since then (only yesterday I took it up again) I have never been able to read that sacred tale without tears. And how much there is in it that is great, mysterious and unfathomable! Afterwards I heard words of mockery and blame, proud words: “How could God give up the most loved of His saints for the amusement of the devil, take away his children, strike him with sore boils so that he scraped the corruption from his sores with a piece of broken pot, and for no purpose except to boast to the devil? ‘See what My saint can suffer for My sake.’” But the greatness of it lies just in the fact that it is a mystery, that the passing earthly show and the eternal truth are brought together in it. In the face of the earthly truth, the eternal truth is accomplished. The Creator, just as on the first days of creation He ended each day with praise: “It is good, what I have created,” looks upon Job and again praises His creation. And Job, praising the Lord, serves not only Him but all His creation, for generations and generations and for ever and ever, since for that he was ordained. Good heavens, what a book it is, and what lessons there are in it! What a book the Bible is, what a miracle, what strength is given with it to man! It is like a mold cast of the world and man and human nature. Everything is there, and a law for everything for all the ages. And what mysteries are solved and revealed! God raises Job up again and gives him wealth again. Many years pass, and he has other children and loves them. But how could he love those new ones when those first children are no more, when he has lost them? Remembering them, how could he be fully happy with the new ones, however dear the new ones might be? But he could, he could. It is the great mystery of human life that old grief passes gradually into quiet, tender joy. The mild serenity of age takes the place of the riotous blood of youth. I bless the rising sun each day, and, as before, my heart sings to meet it. But now I love even more its setting, its long slanting rays, and the soft, tender, gentle memories that come with them, the dear images from the whole of my long, happy life. And over all of it the Divine Truth, softening, reconciling, forgiving! My life is ending, I know that well. But every day that is left to me I feel how my earthly life is in touch with a new, infinite, unknown life, the approaching life, whose nearness sets my soul quivering with rapture, my mind glowing and my heart weeping with joy.

Friends and teachers, I have heard more than once, and lately one hears it more often, that the priests, and above all the village priests, are complaining on all sides about their miserable income and their humiliating lot. They state plainly, even in print (I have read it myself), that they are unable to teach the Scriptures to the people because of the smallness of their means. They say that if Lutherans and heretics come and lead the flock astray, they let them lead it astray, because they have so little to live on. May the Lord increase the sustenance that is so precious to them, for their complaint is just. But truly I say to you, if anyone is to blame in the matter, half the fault is ours. For the priest may be short of time, he may say truly that he is overwhelmed all the while with work and services. But still it is not all his time. Even he has an hour a week to remember God. And he does not work the whole year round. Let him gather the people round him once a week, for an hour in the evening, if only the children at first. The fathers will hear of it and they too will begin to come. There is no need to build halls for this. Let him take them into his own cottage. They will not spoil his cottage, for they would only be there one hour. Let him open that book and begin reading it, without grand words or superciliousness, without condescension to them, but gently and kindly, glad that he is reading to them and that they are listening with attention, loving the words himself, and only stopping from time to time to explain words the peasants do not understand. Do not be anxious, they will understand everything. The Orthodox heart will understand all! Let him read them about Abraham and Sarah, about Isaac and Rebecca, about how Jacob went to Laban and wrestled with the Lord in his dream and said, “This place is holy,” and he will impress the devout mind of the peasant. Let him read, especially to the children, how the brothers sold Joseph, the tender boy, the dreamer and prophet, into bondage, and told their father that a wild beast had devoured him, and showed him his blood-stained clothes. Let him read them how the brothers afterwards journeyed into Egypt for corn, and how Joseph, already a great ruler, unrecognized by them, tormented them, accused them and kept his brother Benjamin, and all through love: “I love you, and loving you I torment you.” For he remembered all his life how they had sold him to the merchants in the burning desert, by the well, and how, wringing his hands, he had wept and begged his brothers not to sell him as a slave in a strange land. And how, seeing them again after many years, he loved them beyond measure, but harassed and tormented them out of love. At last he left them, unable to bear the suffering of his heart, flung himself on his bed and wept. Then, wiping away his tears, he went out to them joyful and told them, “Brothers, I am your brother Joseph!” Let him read them further how happy old Jacob was on learning that his darling boy was still alive, and how he left his own country and went to Egypt, and died in a foreign land. And how he left behind his great prophecy, which had lain mysteriously hidden in his meek and timid heart all his life: that from his offspring, from Judah, would come the great hope of the world, the Messiah and Saviour.

Fathers and teachers, forgive me and do not be angry that, like a little child, I have been babbling about what you have known long ago, and can teach me a hundred times more skillfully. I speak only from rapture, and forgive my tears, for I love the Bible. Let him too weep, the priest of God, and he may be sure that the hearts of his listeners will throb in response. Only a tiny little seed is needed. Drop it into the heart of the peasant and it will not die. It will live in his soul all his life, hidden in the midst of his darkness and sin like a bright spot, like a great reminder. And there is no need of much teaching or explanation. He will understand it all simply. Do you suppose that the peasants do not understand? Try reading them the touching story of the fair Esther and the haughty Vashti, or the miraculous story of Jonah in the whale. Do not forget either the parables of Our Lord. Choose especially from the Gospel of St. Luke (that is what I did), and then from the Acts of the Apostles the conversion of St. Paul (that you must not leave out on any account), and from the _Lives of the Saints_, for instance, the life of Alexey, the man of God, and, greatest of all, the happy martyr and seer of God, Mary of Egypt. With these simple tales you will pierce their hearts. Give one hour a week to it in spite of your poverty, only one little hour. And you will see for yourselves that our people are gracious and grateful, and will repay you a hundredfold. Mindful of the kindness of their priest and the moving words they have heard from him, they will of their own accord help him in his fields and in his house, and will treat him with more respect than before, so that it will even increase his worldly well-being too. The thing is so simple that sometimes one is even afraid to put it into words, for fear of being laughed at. And yet how true it is! One who does not believe in God will not believe in God’s people. He who believes in God’s people will see His Holiness too, even though he had not believed in it till then. Only the people and their future spiritual power will convert our atheists, who have torn themselves away from their native soil.
And what use are Christ’s words, unless we set an example? The people is lost without the Word of God, for its soul is thirsting for the Word and for all that is good.

In my youth, long ago, nearly forty years ago, I traveled all over Russia with Father Anfim, collecting funds for our monastery. One night we stayed on the bank of a great navigable river with some fishermen. A good-looking peasant lad of about eighteen joined us. He had to hurry back next morning to pull a merchant’s barge along the bank. I noticed him looking straight ahead with clear and tender eyes. It was a bright, warm, still night in July. A cool mist rose from the broad river, we could hear the splash of a fish, the birds were quiet, and all was hushed and beautiful, everything praying to God. Only we two were not sleeping, the lad and I, and we talked of the beauty of this world of God’s and of the great mystery of it. Every blade of grass, every insect, ant and golden bee, all know their path so marvelously, though they have no intelligence. They bear witness to the mystery of God and continually accomplish it themselves. I saw that the dear lad’s heart was moved. He told me that he loved the forest and the forest birds. He was a bird-catcher and knew the note of each of them, and could call each bird. “I know nothing better than being in the forest,” said he, “though all things are good.”

“Truly,” I answered him, “all things are good and fair, because all is truth. Look,” said I, “at the horse, that great beast that is so close to man, or at the lowly, thoughtful ox, which feeds him and works for him. Look at their faces: what meekness, what devotion to man, who often beats them mercilessly. What gentleness, what trust and what beauty! It is touching to know that there is no sin in them, for all, all except man, is sinless, and Christ has been with them before us.”
“Why,” asked the boy, “is Christ with them too?”

“It cannot but be so,” said I, “since the Word is for all. All creation and all creatures, every leaf, is striving toward the Word, singing glory to God, weeping to Christ, unconsciously accomplishing this by the mystery of their sinless life. Over there,” said I, “in the forest wanders the dreadful bear, fierce and menacing, and yet innocent in it.” And I told him how once a bear came to a great saint who had taken refuge in a tiny cell in the wood. And the great saint pitied him, went up to him without fear and gave him a piece of bread. “Go along,” said he, “Christ be with you,” and the savage beast walked away meekly and obediently, doing no harm. And the lad was delighted that the bear had walked away without hurting the saint, and that Christ was with him too. “Ah,” said he, “how good that is, how good and beautiful is all God’s work!” He sat musing softly and sweetly. I saw that he understood. And he slept beside me, a light and sinless sleep. May God bless youth! And I prayed for him as I went to sleep. Lord, send peace and light to Your people!
